title: Distributed transactions
lead: Distributed locking, global deadlocks, two-phase commit and recovery.

sections.title: Partitioned data and distributed locking
sections.html:
Lecture context

This lecture extends transactions across nodes. The administrative page describes Edinburgh’s Spring 2026 weeks, an omitted March lecture and the forthcoming theory/parallel topics. These are historical source logistics, not the learner’s current deadlines.

PDF pp. 1–2

One logical database across several machines

Parallel systems assume nearby nodes and fast links; distributed systems must explicitly account for distance, communication delays and failure. Both seek throughput/latency or availability while preserving the logical query result promised by data independence. A transaction can touch several nodes, so local ACID alone cannot ensure they all agree on commit. The lecture proceeds through locking, deadlocks, atomic commit and recovery.

PDF pp. 3–6

Partitioning locks with the data

Assume shared-nothing, partitioned data without replication. A transaction’s arrival node coordinates it. Each data node manages local locks for its pages or tuples. A coarse object such as an entire table spans nodes: assign its lock a home node, partition homes across tables (Sailors,Boats,Reserves), or centralise such locks. The three diagrams compare these placements.

Local lock tables are efficient but do not solve global deadlocks or the final commit/abort decision. A coordinator is a role for one transaction; a machine can coordinate some transactions and participate in others.

PDF pp. 7–12

sections.title: Global deadlocks and commitment
sections.html:
Global deadlock from locally acyclic graphs

Each node sees only its own waits-for edges. Their union can contain T1→T2→T3→T1 even when no individual graph cycles. Periodically send edges to a designated detector, union them, detect a cycle and abort a selected transaction across its participants. Detection is about a consistent enough view of current waits: stale delayed reports need care in a production protocol.

PDF pp. 13–15

Failures, delayed messages and unanimous voting

A failed node must recover in a world where other nodes may have advanced. Messages can be delayed, reordered within/between channels or appear lost. A timeout cannot establish whether the remote node failed or merely replied slowly.

Atomic commit asks every participant to reach the same outcome. Commit requires every participant’s YES, because any node may detect a constraint violation or be unable to commit. A majority of data participants cannot overrule a NO in this transaction model. Voting needs durable promises and a recoverable decision, not just collecting transient replies.

PDF pp. 16–21

sections.title: Two-phase commit protocol
sections.html:
Phase one: prepare and vote

2PC is two-phase commit, distinct from 2PL. The coordinator sends PREPARE(T1) to each participant. Each checks whether it can make its local part durable and later obey the final decision; it returns YES or NO. Commit requires YES from all participants. A NO or a missing vote before a decision permits the coordinator to choose abort.

A YES is a promise to remain prepared, not a local commit. A prepared participant must retain the information and locks required to finish either way. The successive diagrams show sends, network transit and delivery of all YES votes; transit and receipt are different states.

PDF pp. 22–27

Phase two: decision and acknowledgment

After its decision is durable, the coordinator sends COMMIT or ABORT to everyone. Participants apply that same outcome, persist it and acknowledge. ACK means the decision has been processed durably; it does not replace the earlier YES vote. Repeated or delayed phase-two messages must reproduce the same decision rather than create a second outcome.

PDF pp. 28–30

sections.title: Persistent protocol state
sections.html:
Log order before a YES and before COMMIT

On PREPARE, a participant appends PREPARE (or ABORT), including its coordinator identity, and flushes before sending the vote. The source participant log uses 010:<T1,PREPARE>. The coordinator waits for all YES votes, appends its COMMIT record including participant identities, and flushes before sending any COMMIT. Its illustrated record is 080:<T1,COMMIT>.

If the coordinator crashes after the flush but before a send, the durable record still fixes commit. If it crashes before recording a decision, participants cannot infer commit from their own YES votes. The animation separates append-in-memory from flush-to-disk at each role.

PDF pp. 31–38

Participant completion and coordinator END

After receiving COMMIT, a participant appends its decision (source 020:<T1,COMMIT>), flushes it and sends ACK. After all ACKs the coordinator records transaction END (090:<T1,TXN-END>) to finish bookkeeping. ABORT follows the chosen presumed-abort logging convention.

The protocol’s critical durable-before-send chain is: participant PREPARE→YES; coordinator decision→COMMIT/ABORT; participant decision→ACK. The source’s asterisks mark required waits for log flush. END says completion work is done; it is not the moment that first makes an already durable COMMIT true.

PDF pp. 39–48

sections.title: Recovery, strict locking and blocking
sections.html:
Recovery by role and durable state

Before voting YES a participant can abort its unfinished local work; after a durable PREPARE it must learn the final outcome. A coordinator missing a vote can abort before choosing commit; one waiting for a commit ACK must retry completion rather than reverse its decision. ARIES analysis can hand these transactions to background recovery processes.

Role and durable recordsAction
Coordinator: COMMIT + ENDNo outstanding completion work
Coordinator: COMMIT onlyResend phase-two decision; collect acknowledgments
Coordinator: ABORTPresumed-abort cleanup
Participant: no PREPARE/decisionNo commitment promise; abort local incomplete work
Participant: PREPARE + COMMITRetain commit and send ACK
Participant: PREPARE onlyInquire; wait for authoritative decision
Participant: ABORTAbort cleanup; no commit

In the source’s presumed-abort protocol, an inquiry to a recovered coordinator with no decision state receives ABORT. A durable COMMIT requires phase two to complete even after restart. A prepared participant without a final decision must inquire and wait; a timeout alone cannot justify unilateral abort.

PDF pp. 49–54

Combining 2PC with strict 2PL

Number messages densely per sender/receiver/transaction. If message k+1 arrives before k, buffer it until the gap is filled. When processing the final decision, all required earlier lock requests must have been processed. Coordinate the durable decision, local undo where needed and lock release so uncommitted effects do not escape.

The source’s “safe local abort” statement applies where the protocol permits abort; it cannot override a participant’s prepared promise or a recorded global commit. Dense sequence numbering addresses ordering, not arbitrary permanent message loss by itself.

PDF p. 55

Blocking and the limits of classic 2PC

If the coordinator’s outcome is unavailable, prepared participants can remain in doubt holding locks, making some data unavailable. Recovery assumes nodes and their durable logs eventually return. Not every failure blocks every execution, but an unfortunate coordinator failure can block a transaction indefinitely under the classic assumptions.

2PC solves atomic commitment with unanimous participant voting; it is not by itself a generally available fault-tolerant consensus service. The lecture mentions three-phase commit and Paxos Commit as further approaches, without teaching their full algorithms. More nodes increase failure exposure, which makes this availability issue material to scale-out.

PDF pp. 56–57

quiz.question: A participant has only a durable PREPARE record and loses contact with the coordinator. What is safe?
options: Commit independently because it voted YES
Abort immediately when a timeout expires
Seek the decision; it may have to wait
Delete the log and start over
quiz.explanation: A YES vote is a promise to follow the common decision. The coordinator may already have committed elsewhere.

source.summary: Lecture 22 studies partitioned, nonreplicated data, distributed locking, global deadlock, two-phase commit, and the coordination of logging with recovery. Two-phase commit can block progress when the coordinator is unreachable.

limitations: The lecture assumes partitioning without replication. Consensus-based improvements are mentioned but not developed in detail.
